before: The immunopeptidome is a biological repertoire in a defined cell population and context; an immunopeptidomics list is a method-dependent subset recovered and identified from a sample. Class I and class II repertoires are separate, and a protein can be abundant while a derived peptide is poorly generated, loaded or retained. Inflammatory signals changed peptide patterns in cancer cell lines (Chong et al., 2018, ovarian cancer cells and interferon gamma, PMID 29242379; Javitt et al., 2019, lung cancer cells and TNF-alpha and interferon gamma acting through HLA-B, PMID 30833945), which shows context-dependent remodelling and not that inflammation adds useful targets. Whole-lysate capture can recover intracellular as well as surface complexes, mixed tissue adds cancer, immune and stromal sources, relative instrument intensity is not surface copies per cell, and a reported sequence can be misassigned (Wilhelm et al., 2021, PMID 34099720). Method B identifying 1,200 peptides against method A's 800 (fictional) shows no biological difference. Sarkizova et al. (2020) gives allele-dependent repertoires from mono-allelic lines.

In a fictional comparison, method B identifies 1,200 peptides against method A's 800: 400 more, or 50% more identified peptides. That count difference does not establish 50% more biological display, any recovery fraction or a clinical threshold. Sarkizova et al. (2020) gives allele-dependent repertoires from mono-allelic lines.

Source-protein supply, processing, loading and turnover can change the repertoire. Keep the biological claim attached to the cell population, specimen site and time, cell state, HLA class and alleles. A recovered list from one preparation does not describe every site, time or cell in a tumour. State the capture reagent, recovery, searchable sequences and identification threshold alongside the list, and request the method's material consumption and analysis cost before using a scarce specimen.
proposals.reason: Correct the fictional count comparison without asserting biological equality; retain every other existing note sentence and add the missing specimen-context reading rule.

before: Reading guide (OnCo inference). In a mixed specimen a recovered HLA-associated peptide does not reveal its cell of origin or its abundance on living cell surfaces. Non-detection does not show biological absence: it also reflects capture, allele coverage, the searchable sequence set and instrument and software sensitivity, and detection does not show safe tumour recognition. No source read here establishes that formalin-fixed tissue is usable for an assay validated on cells or frozen tissue; the lesson's statement that one protocol proposed an adaptation could not be checked (publisher page unavailable), so that claim is withheld and compatibility must be shown for the named method.

Fictional worked example. A specimen yields peptide A but not peptide B. A has measured support in that preparation. For B, ask whether its allele was recovered, whether the altered sequence was searchable and whether sensitivity was adequate; 'A detected, B absent everywhere' is stronger than the experiment supports. If B is simply missing from the search database it could not have been identified as configured, so its absence is not a clean biological negative, and correcting the database does not by itself guarantee recovery or prove natural display.

Reading guide: binding prediction estimates a model output, whereas immunopeptidomics identifies recovered peptides, and total-protein measurements are a different question from HLA-associated fragments (a protein can be abundant without any of its peptides being displayed, an inference); presentation, immune response and efficacy are three separate claims.

Measurement card in words (a reading guide). Input: which tissue preparation and preservation are compatible, and how much material is consumed. Output and units: peptide identities and unique-sequence counts; instrument intensities are method-dependent and not copies per cell. Identification threshold: the sequence database, the false-discovery rule (spectrum or peptide level) and the supporting spectra. Coverage: which HLA classes and alleles were captured and which allele assignments were measured or inferred. Material and cost: protocol-specific input, preservation, consumption, turnaround and analysis cost, requested before a scarce specimen is used. Validation: recovery, reproducibility and reference-peptide checks for the method. Failure modes: low input, poor recovery, mixed cell populations, database gaps and wrong sequence assignments. Limits: non-detection does not prove absence and detection does not prove safe recognition; there is no universal tissue requirement or detection threshold.

In the illustrated immunoaffinity workflow, antibodies on beads capture peptide-bearing HLA complexes from prepared lysate. This is laboratory recovery after sample preparation, rather than antibody attack on living cells. Release and separation are different steps: acid dissociates the complex, and subsequent purification separates the peptides from other material before chromatography and mass spectrometry. Acid release alone does not establish a peptide-only input. The peptides remain connected amino-acid chains; this workflow identifies the recovered fragments rather than digesting them into free amino acids. Chong and colleagues' methods describe lysate capture, acid elution, solid-phase purification and peptide LC-MS analysis. Purcell and colleagues' protocol abstract describes immunoaffinity capture, acid denaturation, peptide extraction and HPLC separation before identification. These named workflows do not define a universal protocol or a complete surface census.
proposals.reason: Append the physical preparation/capture/release/separation distinction to the existing method owner, preserving every prior note, link and scalar.
